 Delegation From Allied Gardens, San Diego 
 The Republic of Latvia

 Housing Insecurity for Children 
 Throughout the world, many children are exposed to the detrimental effects of housing 
 insecurity, but in comparison with other European Union member states, child poverty and social 
 exclusion indicators for the Republic of Latvia are among the highest.  1  People facing housing 
 insecurity can meet a variety of problems such as being unable to pay rent, overcrowding, moving 
 frequently, homelessness, and spending a large amount of household income on housing.  2  Housing 
 insecurity significantly affects children because it can disrupt their education, have adverse physical 
 and mental health effects, and disrupt a child’s development at a critical time. The 1959 United 
 Nations Declaration of the Rights of the Child (UNDRC) defines all child's rights to protection, 
 shelter, education, and healthcare, but these can be jeopardized because of insecurity. In addition to 
 the declaration, the 1989 Convention on the Rights of the Child guides the  United Nations Childrens 
 Fund (UNICEF)  mission to further the rights of the child.  3  Data shows that moving frequently can 
 significantly impact a child’s health, one of the rights defined in the UNDRC. If a child is born while 
 the family is experiencing a period of housing instability, it can lower the infant's birth weight, cause 
 respiratory problems such as asthma, a fever, and other health problems that, if left untreated, can 
 stay with the child forever.  4  Further, moving three or more times in early childhood, especially for 
 low-income children, can be detrimental to a child's cognitive, mental, and emotional development.

 This can be devastating to a child’s development because 90 percent of the brain develops before the 
 age of five and constant moving can impede brain development at such an early age.  5  Housing 
 insecurity, especially poverty and homelessness, also affects education. Students who move 
 frequently and experience homelessness are twice as likely to become “chronically absent,” meaning 
 that a student is absent at least ten percent of the school year. This has been proven to result in poor 
 academic performance, and it inhibits development which is crucial to the child.  6 
 As previously stated, child poverty and social exclusion are preeminent issues children in 
 Latvia deal with daily. This is an immense issue because as of 2019, about 19 percent of children in 
 Latvia were at risk of poverty or social exclusion. Further, although the Latvian Ministry of Welfare 
 regrets not developing an adequate plan to help keep children out of poverty during the COVID-19 
 pandemic, mitigating the fatal virus was of utmost importance. Having said this, the lack of a 
 thorough plan further exacerbated the public health and education crisis, especially for children 
 living in or at risk of poverty. This left the aid in the hands of non-governmental organizations 
 (NGOs) who were overwhelmed by the increased demand for aid caused by COVID-19. This caused 
 an abundance of issues for children in the Republic of Latvia such as an increase in “violent 
 episodes” with families, limited access to healthcare services, educational challenges, and an increase 
 in mental health issues.  7 
 Heightened by the COVID-19 pandemic, this wide range of issues inflamed by housing 
 insecurity can have an enduring impact on a child’s life. Aggravating this, a study conducted in 
 Canada has shown that overcrowded households have an increased risk of tuberculosis and infectious

 cognitive development which can lead to substance abuse.  8  Further, abuse can cause a child to enter 
 the foster care system (FCS), another form of housing insecurity. In regards to a child’s risk of 
 poverty in Latvia, although 29.4 percent of families with one adult and children are at risk of poverty, 
 there has been a steady decline in this percentage partially due to the Republic of Latvia providing 
 families with 500 Euros per child in 2020 to help families during the pandemic.  9  Furthermore, the 
 2012 Latvian ACE study, a study measuring different types of childhood neglect, abuse, and 
 maltreatment showed that only 16.9 percent of respondents reported not having any traumatic or 
 adverse experiences during childhood (ages 0-14). This is further proven by a study conducted by the 
 Ombudsman’s Office which deals with human rights in Latvia. The study included 500 children in 
 grades 5-12 and found that 47 percent of the children had experienced some form of violence in their 
 childhood.  10  Maltreatment can be exceedingly harmful to children with a high ACE score because it 
 is linked with earlier sexual intercourse, higher odds of using drugs, and an increased risk of suicide. 
 11  Even worse, a study has found that those who have experienced at least two forms of childhood 
 maltreatment are 180% more likely to be living below the poverty line in adulthood.  12  Finally, the 
 University of Nevada, Las Vegas has conducted a study that shows that in low-income households 
 that do not know how the rent will be paid, there is an increase in maltreatment. This shows that 
 housing insecurity can have a direct impact on childhood maltreatment.  13

 Section II 
 In 2007, nearly 40 percent of Latvians were cost-burdened, meaning that they spent over 40 
 percent of their disposable income on housing costs. In 2020, only about 7 percent of people living in 
 Latvia were cost burdened  14  Although this number has  decreased significantly, there is still work to 
 be done. Studies show that communities experience a rapid increase in homelessness when  a typical 
 household spends at least 32 percent of their disposable income on rent.  15  Further research has shown 
 that the average Latvian household spends 11.8 percent of their disposable income on housing, but 
 single-parent households on average spend 16.4 percent of their disposable income on housing.  16 
 Furthermore, 35 out of every 10,000 Latvians are homeless, much higher than the rates of Latvia’s 
 closest neighbors and allies such as Lithuania and Estonia. From 2009 to 2017, following the Great 
 Recession, there was a 389 percent increase in Latvia’s homeless population. Part of the reason why 
 homelessness in Latvia is high is that measures to reduce it are mainly left up to individual 
 jurisdictions, and there is a significant amount of prejudice against homeless people preventing them 
 from attaining healthcare and access to food and water.  17  Although there is no official legislation in 
 Latvian law that discusses homelessness, recent measures have been taken to fight homelessness by 
 providing shelters. These actions have been beneficial to families, which helps to keep kids off the 
 streets. Although the Republic of Latvia has made progress in providing shelters for people facing 
 homelessness, no progress has been made to provide affordable housing. Although long-term 
 solutions have not yet been made to transition people from off the streets and out of shelters to living 
 in affordable housing and working, there has been a decrease in the number of children who are

 homeless. This is likely because the Ministry of Welfare has provided targeted relief to families to 
 lower the number of children facing homelessness, especially in the capital, Riga.  18  In recent years, 
 social services in Latvia have included day shelters for families and extra support for orphaned 
 children and those living with non-family members. This indicates that Latvia is making progress 
 because child poverty reduction has never historically been a priority. Furthermore, in normative acts, 
 children are identified as a priority group to receive special support services, but requirements such 
 as adequate healthcare and housing are often not met. A first step for Latvia would be to address 
 inadequate housing supply and poor housing quality in future country reports. 
 Additionally, the number of kids in care institutions has been gradually declining, but this 
 number remains very high. Care institutions can cause children to suffer from structural neglect, 
 which includes minimal resources and inadequate social-emotional interactions between caregivers 
 and children. This can lead to malnourishment and cause children to have “post-institutional 
 syndrome” which has the potential to negatively impact or delay their physical, hormonal, cognitive, 
 and emotional development.  19 
 Although 70 percent of households in Latvia own their house outright, which allows for 
 greater housing stability, most of the purchases were made during the Soviet era, so many of these 
 homes are in poor condition. This is extremely problematic because studies have shown that children 
 living in low-income households are more developmentally harmed from poor housing quality than 
 residential instability (constant moving) or affordability issues.  20  Even worse, over one-third of 
 households live in overcrowded dwellings, which is the highest percentage of any OECD member.  21

 Further, a study was conducted that  tracked children in rural areas who faced poor living conditions 
 such as overcrowding, clutter, and hazards in the dwelling beginning at age 9. The study found that 
 after fifteen years of living in these poor conditions, children had worse psychological health and 
 they had feelings of helplessness. This is a major problem in Latvia because of the very high number 
 of households that live in poor conditions or in overcrowded dwellings (over half of all children live 
 in overcrowded dwellings throughout Latvia).  22 
 The Republic of Latvia has yet to formally make the reduction of a child’s risk of poverty a 
 targeted priority, but the government has launched campaigns to lower poverty numbers. However, 
 the National Reform Programme of Latvia (NRP) (also referred to as the “Europe 2020” strategy) 
 aims to reduce poverty index numbers for the whole population to 21 percent, but this does not 
 specifically target children. Alternatively, the NRP does target the reduction of child poverty 
 differently by aiming to reduce labor force taxes, ensuring the accessibility of free primary and 
 secondary education, and reducing income inequality. Furthermore, Latvia’s guaranteed minimum 
 income (GMI) benefits have been increased by fifteen percent for families with children who have 
 not.  23  Latvia has been very successful with lowering  at-risk-of-poverty-or-social-exclusion (AROPE) 
 levels by aggressively following the Europe 2020 strategy, but two-thirds of nations have not. Latvia 
 urges other European Nation members to actively follow the Europe 2020 strategy. 
 Section III 
 To lessen the impacts of housing insecurity on all children, it is necessary to provide 
 affordable housing to families.  Article 96 of the  Latvian Constitution states that every child shall 
 have the right to housing. Additionally, Latvia has signed many binding international treaties and 
 agreements such as the European Social Charter to provide adequate housing, lower housing costs,

 guarantee to households with children. This legislation has been shown to benefit higher-income 
 households the most because they have the income to support the mortgage  25  The Delegation of 
 Latvia believes there should be housing support for families that do not qualify for a mortgage 
 through government grants. These grants could go to families who are beginning to enter the labor 
 force but do not yet have the means to purchase a home suitable for their family and single-parent 
 households as they are significantly disadvantaged by housing insecurity because they are at a higher 
 risk of poverty than dual-income households. The grants must have restrictions on the size of the 
 house based on family size and whether the parent is part of the labor force. Families would apply 
 through an updated page on the Latvia Portal of State Administration Services website. The 
 eligibility requirements would be determined by Latvia’s GMI benefit criteria and new criteria to 
 include the “missing middle.” Applications would be reviewed by municipal social service offices. 
 Any member of the family can file a claim, but there should be proof that you are entering the 
 workforce if you are a dual-income household. Additionally, there shall be support services available 
 to families that are not yet working to help them find jobs. Latvia also has a social housing unit 
 which is controlled by local housing municipalities and the Ministry of Regional Development. The 
 social houses and apartments are municipally owned and local authorities are responsible for funding 
 the social housing, although partnerships with the private sector are encouraged. Latvia has one of 
 the lowest amounts of social housing stock in the OECD.  26  Additionally, housing allowances are very 
 low; a family with a single earner and two children would receive about seven percent of their gross 
 earnings for a housing allowance, which is less than half of the average received in other OECD

 countries. Not only are the social housing stock and allowances minimal, but they also leave out the 
 homeless population and the households that cannot afford mortgages but are not disadvantaged 
 enough to qualify for social housing (the “missing middle”). Further, the Republic of Latvia has yet 
 to create a formal plan to combat homelessness, so developing a specific plan to reduce homelessness 
 in the nation should be a top priority of the government. The Delegation of Latvia believes Latvia 
 should leverage funds from the European Commission’s Affordable Housing Initiative to create more 
 social housing, refurbish existing social dwellings, and fund the grants.  27 
 Since a big problem in Latvia is the quality of housing as opposed to the availability of 
 housing, it is in the country's best interest to “refurbish” homes rather than build new ones. Ten 
 percent of children in Latvia have self-reported not having access to basic facilities, which is a very 
 high number in comparison to other OECD members, showing the poor quality of housing in Latvia. 
 It is important to note that there is a similar housing situation in the two other Baltic Region nations. 
 A nationwide survey should be conducted to find out which residential dwellings are in poor 
 condition and who needs access to government aid services. After the survey is completed, we feel as 
 if the government should partner with the private sector to improve the already existing properties. 
 The amount of aid a household receives should be based on criteria close to what is used by the EU. 
 In addition, we believe there should be an expansion in rent allowances to 1, allow for 
 “missing middle” households to benefit while also remaining in the workforce, and 2, allow for 
 necessary home refurbishment to take place by partially paying for the construction costs. The 
 Delegation of Latvia understands the value of education on a child’s emotional and physical 
 development and thus believes that families whose kids attend school at least ninety percent of the 
 time should receive additional benefits, especially remittances for construction and rent.

 Finally, there have been very few initiatives by the private or public sectors to promote 
 parenting education in Latvia.  28  Parenting education  is important because improving parenting skills 
 enhances a child's well-being. Although Latvia has created the Latvian National Development Plan 
 2021-2027 to provide parenting education we feel that it is still inadequate because these measures 
 are mainly in Urban areas. This leaves out the parents in rural areas where parenting education may 
 be needed the most. We think that if there have been any reports of abuse or a child has been 
 chronically absent from school, parenting classes should be required to receive housing assistance. 
 We believe that with collaboration between the private and public sectors, increased social housing 
 and allowances, a partnership between education and housing, and an increased effort to provide 
 affordable housing, housing insecurity can be reduced for children living in the Republic of Latvia.

 Finally, there have been very few initiatives by the private or public sectors to promote 
 parenting education in Latvia.  28  Parenting education  is important because improving parenting skills

 2021-2027 to provide parenting education we feel that it is still inadequate because these measures

 chronically absent from school, parenting classes should be required to receive housing assistance.
